scope_note: External audio classifiers — the models that decide whether a sound should reach the agent at all, and what it is. Every neighbouring section answers a question about the words or the speaker; this one does not. Listening transcribes it, Turns decides whether the user has finished, Speakerid decides who spoke, Wake word listens for one fixed phrase, and Speech enhancement cleans it up first. Attention covers addressee detection, audio-event and scene tagging, paralinguistic classification, and the backbone architectures underneath them. The dividing line against Turns is a single question — Turns asks whether the user has finished, Attention asks whether this should interrupt anything.
method_note: Nothing here is benchmarked by OpenGauntlet. Figures come from primary sources — vendor docs, model cards, repositories, and papers — and every accuracy figure is quoted with the test set it was measured on, because in this domain every headline number carries a different denominator and none of them are comparable. One further caveat specific to this section: the governed research corpus behind it is thinner here than for Voices or Listening, so more of these rows rest on vendor documentation and repository evidence than on peer-reviewed papers, and rows say which. This edition's 31 new rows were built one research pass per category, each followed by an adversarial auditor instructed to refute rather than confirm every figure against its primary source; the corrections below are what that process struck.

systems.name: Adaptive Knowledge Distillation for Device-Directed Speech Detection (Apple)
systems.task: Binary device-directed classification across THREE invocation types (two keyword-triggered variants plus a keyword-free follow-up case) from a compact transformer or conformer student, trained with task-specific adapters that distil a frozen, general-purpose ASR acoustic encoder.
systems.availability: No released weights or code — a research paper only, evaluated on in-house training and evaluation sets.
systems.best_for: The most recent (2025) published data point on how far knowledge distillation can push a compact, deployable DDSD student — and the only row here that reports accuracy separately across three distinct invocation types from one distillation recipe.
systems.watch: In-house-only data throughout, no dataset name or size breakdown beyond "2.7k hours," and no released model — reproducing this requires both a frozen general-purpose ASR encoder and a comparably sized DDSD corpus of your own.
systems.standout: Generalizes across transformer AND conformer student architectures with the same adapter-based distillation recipe, rather than reporting a result tied to one architecture choice.
systems.architecture: Frozen general-purpose ASR pretrained acoustic encoder (teacher) with task-specific adapters, distilled jointly with a compact transformer/conformer student trained on DDSD.
systems.accuracy_note: Best (adaptive KD, Conformer student) EER: 1.05% on the primary keyword invocation set (vs 1.57% baseline without distillation, ≈33% relative improvement — the paper's own ≈26% figure is a Conformer-wide average across HAG+AG combined, not this specific pairing) and 8.70% on the keyword-free follow-up set (vs 10.87% baseline, ≈19% relative improvement); a secondary keyword-variant set improves from 5.24% to 4.19% EER. Trained on 2.7k hours of in-house audio spanning all three invocation types; evaluated on the paper's own in-house per-invocation-type sets. Not comparable to any other row on this page.
systems.training_data: 2.7k hours in-house audio spanning three invocation types.
systems.verification_note: Read in full via arXiv HTML primary source (arxiv.org/html/2508.02801v1), including the exact Table 1 EER figures.

systems.name: Adaptive Speaker Embedding Self-Augmentation for PVAD
systems.licence: Not established from the sources reviewed
systems.task: Per-frame target-speaker detection, as in Personal VAD, but addressing the case where the ENROLLMENT clip is short (e.g. a single wake word) — augments the enrollment speaker embedding by additively fusing keyframe embeddings pulled from the mixed input speech itself, then iteratively refines that embedding as detection proceeds.
systems.availability: The paper states source code is available at an anonymized double-blind review repository (4open.science); this has not been verified to persist as a public, deanonymized release now that the paper is accepted.
systems.best_for: The specific, practical failure mode every wake-word-triggered personal-VAD deployment has — enrollment audio is typically as short as the wake word itself — and a proposed fix that does not require re-enrolling with a longer clip.
systems.watch: ICASSP-2026-accepted and very recent (submitted 2026-01); the numeric results were not available in the reviewed abstract, and the "source code available" claim points at an anonymous review-time repository whose post-publication persistence is unverified — do not assume a downloadable release exists yet.
systems.standout: Iteratively refines the target-speaker embedding DURING detection rather than treating enrollment as a one-shot, fixed reference — every other speaker-conditioned row on this page uses a static enrollment embedding.
systems.architecture: Speaker-embedding self-augmentation via additive keyframe fusion from mixed speech, plus an iterative long-term embedding-adaptation loop during detection.
systems.accuracy_note: Abstract reports "significant gains in recall, precision, and F1-score under short enrollment conditions, matching full-length enrollment performance after five iterative updates" but does not state the numeric values or the dataset in the portion reviewed — treat as a qualitative, not a quantitative, claim until the full text is read.
systems.verification_note: Abstract read via the arXiv primary source (arxiv.org/abs/2601.12769); full text, exact figures, and the claimed code repository were not independently confirmed.

systems.name: Device-Directed Speech Detection for Follow-up Conversations (Apple)
systems.task: Binary device-directed confidence for a FOLLOW-UP utterance issued without repeating the wake word, conditioned on the ASR text and ASR-confidence signal of the PRECEDING query, via LLM prompting or a binary classification head on top of an LLM.
systems.availability: No released weights, code, or dataset — a research paper only.
systems.best_for: The published case for why an addressee classifier needs conversational memory — modelling the prior turn's content and ASR confidence is what drives the reported gain, not the follow-up audio in isolation.
systems.watch: The internal follow-up dataset is unnamed and not published; the reported gain is relative to the paper's own no-context ablation, not to any other system here, and nothing is downloadable.
systems.standout: Directly targets the follow-up-turn case that SAS's own related-work section (Table 9's neighbouring discussion) flags as a distinct problem from the single, first-utterance case every other row on this page evaluates.
systems.architecture: Pretrained LLM prompted with, or fine-tuned as a classifier over, the current follow-up utterance's ASR text plus the prior query's ASR text and decoder-confidence signal.
systems.accuracy_note: Best configuration (ClassHead, full prior-query context, 8-best ASR hypotheses) reaches EER 7.9% and a false-accept rate of 4.8% at a fixed 10% false-reject rate — a 20-40% relative reduction in false alarms versus modelling the follow-up utterance alone — on the paper's own ≈245k-segment internal dataset built from ≈19k recordings across 1,300 English-speaking participants.
systems.training_data: ≈245k utterance-pair segments from ≈19k internal audio recordings, 1,300 demographically diverse English-native participants, device-directed to non-directed ratio ≈1:4.
systems.languages_note: English-native participant pool only, per the paper's dataset description.
systems.verification_note: Read in full via arXiv HTML primary source (arxiv.org/html/2411.00023v1), including the exact FAR/EER figures and dataset description; not indexed in the governed research corpus.

systems.name: Device-Directed Speech Detection — Regularization via Distillation (Apple)
systems.task: Binary device-directed classification for touch-based invocation, from an acoustic-only model trained on WEAKLY-labelled data and regularized by knowledge distillation from an ASR-transcript-based teacher (LatticeRNN) — a training recipe, not a new architecture.
systems.availability: No released weights or code — a research paper only, evaluated on an anonymized, short-lived in-house touch-invocation dataset.
systems.best_for: The published argument for why an addressee classifier does not need fully human-labelled training data — the distilled acoustic-only student closes most of the gap to an ASR-transcript-dependent teacher using weak labels alone.
systems.watch: Test set is described only as "anonymized and short-lived" with no public release; a 2025 follow-up from an overlapping author list (Adaptive Knowledge Distillation, arXiv 2508.02801) generalizes the same distillation idea to a frozen general-purpose ASR encoder plus task adapters, reporting further EER gains of +26%/+19% across three invocation types on its own in-house set.
systems.standout: The acoustic-only student, after distillation, needs no ASR transcript at inference time yet approaches the accuracy of a teacher that does — useful wherever running ASR just to gate whether ASR should run is the thing you are trying to avoid.
systems.architecture: Acoustic-only false-trigger-mitigation (AFTM) student regularized via knowledge distillation from an ASR-lattice-based teacher (LRNN); only the dev/test splits are human-labelled, the training data is weak-labelled.
systems.accuracy_note: Distilled acoustic model (AFTM-D) reaches 6.2% EER versus 18.4% for the undistilled acoustic baseline (AFTM) — a ≈66% relative improvement — and fusing AFTM-D with the LRNN teacher reaches 4.0% EER, a further ≈20% relative gain over the LRNN teacher alone, on the paper's own anonymized in-house touch-invocation dev/test set.
systems.verification_note: Read in full via arXiv HTML primary source (arxiv.org/html/2203.15975), including the exact Table 2 EER figures.

systems.name: FireRedChat streaming personalized VAD (pVAD)
systems.licence: Not applicable — pVAD weights not released (sibling components FireRedASR and FireRedTTS are separately open-sourced on GitHub; pVAD is not)
systems.task: Streaming per-frame target-speaker gate that suppresses barge-in triggers from non-primary speakers and background noise while passing primary-speaker barge-ins through, feeding a full-duplex turn-taking controller.
systems.availability: Described only as "internal models" in a shipped, demoed system (FireRedChat); no standalone pVAD weights, code, or checkpoint are published.
systems.best_for: The strongest evidence that speaker-conditioned gating measurably changes a real barge-in problem — the ~3x false-barge-in-rate reduction over a same-team, same-dataset non-speaker-conditioned baseline isolates what target-speaker conditioning buys.
systems.watch: The 10.2% figure is a whole-system result (pVAD feeding a barge-in decision), not an isolated pVAD accuracy number, and pVAD itself has no published weights despite FireRedASR/FireRedTTS from the same team being open-sourced — do not assume this component is available just because its siblings are. FireRedChat's end-of-turn detector is a separate model and belongs to the Turns section, not here.
systems.standout: The comparison is same-dataset, same-team, held everything else fixed except speaker conditioning — the closest thing on this page to a controlled ablation of "does knowing the target speaker actually help barge-in filtering".
systems.architecture: Speaker-embedding-conditioned streaming VAD, evaluated as one component of FireRedChat's turn-taking controller alongside a separate end-of-turn detector.
systems.accuracy_note: System-level result (attributable to pVAD's speaker gating, not an isolated pVAD-only ablation): 10.2% false barge-in rate at a T90 latency of 170 ms, versus 33.4% false barge-in rate at 140 ms T90 for a LiveKit + Silero-VAD baseline with no speaker conditioning, and 78.1% for a Ten-VAD baseline. Measured on the paper's own 2,000-utterance synthetic barge-in test set (1,000 Chinese + 1,000 English), with injected background noise (5 dB SNR) and a secondary competing speaker (20 dB SNR) around the primary speaker's speech.
systems.verification_note: Read in full via the governed Imprynt research corpus (9-conversational-dynamics/2509.06502), pages 7-9, including Table 1/2 figures.

systems.name: Multimodal Device-Directed Speech Detection (Apple/TH Nürnberg)
systems.task: Binary device-directed vs. non-directed confidence per utterance, fusing acoustic-encoder features (Whisper or CLAP), the ASR 1-best transcript, and ASR decoder confidence signals as prefix tokens into a frozen or LoRA-adapted LLM classifier.
systems.availability: No released weights, code, or trained model — a research paper only, evaluated on a proprietary Apple dataset.
systems.best_for: Reading before building an LLM-fused addressee classifier — the paper's own audio-only/text-only/multimodal ablation is the clearest published breakdown of where the signal actually comes from.
systems.watch: Every figure is measured on an unnamed, proprietary Apple dataset with no public benchmark comparison, and nothing here is downloadable — budget for collecting your own labelled device-directed corpus before this recipe is usable. A closely related NeurIPS-2023-workshop paper by the same authors (arXiv 2312.03632) shows a lower-data, resource-constrained variant of the same idea reaching comparable EER gains from as few as 80k training examples.
systems.standout: Multimodal fusion beats both single-modality baseline by a wide, ablated margin, and scaling the LLM plus LoRA compounds a further double-digit relative EER cut on top of that — the gains are additive, not redundant.
systems.architecture: Pretrained LLM backbone (GPT-2 through 1.5B) consuming acoustic-encoder and ASR-decoder features as prefix tokens ahead of the ASR 1-best text; fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation in the larger configurations.
systems.accuracy_note: EER 7.45% for the best multimodal configuration (CLAP backbone), against 19.13% audio-only (CLAP) and 12.15% text-only — a 61% and 39% relative improvement respectively — on the paper's own ≈35-hour, ≈37k-utterance in-house evaluation set (≈14k device-directed, ≈23k non-directed). A further LoRA-tuned 1.5B-parameter LLM configuration reaches EER 6.53%/8.41% depending on backbone. Not comparable to any other row on this page.
systems.training_data: ≈40k directed + ≈40k non-directed utterances (≈126 hours) of randomized, anonymized near-field device audio, plus a ≈3M-utterance ASR-transcribed text corpus for the text-only ablation.
systems.verification_note: Read in full via the governed Imprynt research corpus (13-latest-voice-2026/2403.14438), including Table 1/2 EER figures.

systems.name: Personal VAD
systems.task: Per-frame three-way output — non-speech, target-speaker speech, non-target-speaker speech — conditioned on an enrolled speaker embedding. The signal that separates the primary user from a side conversation.
systems.availability: No official weights. Published architecture only; reimplementable on top of any speaker-embedding model.
systems.best_for: The reference formulation for target-speaker VAD, and the thing most of the addressee stack is quietly a reimplementation of.
systems.watch: There are no weights to download. Budget for training it, and note that speaker identity is not addressee — the primary user side-talking and the primary user interrupting are the same speaker.
systems.standout: Reframes voice activity detection as a three-way speaker-conditioned question rather than a binary one, which is what makes side-talk separable at all.
systems.architecture: Speaker-conditioned streaming VAD, designed for on-device use

systems.name: Personal VAD 2.0 (Google)
systems.task: Per-frame three-way output — non-speech, target-speaker speech, non-target-speaker speech — as in the original Personal VAD, redesigned for production use with enrollment AND enrollment-less operation, streaming inference, and a quantized on-device footprint.
systems.availability: No released weights or code — a research paper only, evaluated inside Google's internal streaming ASR pipeline.
systems.best_for: The production-readiness case study for target-speaker VAD — it is the one entry on this page that reports impact on a full downstream ASR pipeline rather than an isolated classifier metric, and it explicitly solves the short-enrollment (wake-word-length) problem the original Personal VAD left open.
systems.watch: No weights or code released, same as the original Personal VAD; the headline WER numbers are downstream-pipeline effects, not the model's own EER, so they are not comparable to any other classifier's accuracy_note here.
systems.standout: Reports an enrollment-LESS mode that matches the non-personalized baseline's WER on regular queries while still cutting side-talk insertions when a target speaker is enrolled — the same model covers both cases rather than requiring a separate deployment per scenario.
systems.model_size: 1.0 MB after 8-bit quantization on a Conformer backbone (parameter count not stated in the paper).
systems.architecture: Speaker-embedding-modulated streaming detector (FiLM-conditioned) with a Conformer backbone; a training paradigm to generalize to enrollment-less conditions; 8-bit weight quantization for the on-device deployment.
systems.accuracy_note: Measured end-to-end as downstream ASR word error rate rather than a standalone EER: on a concatenated multi-speaker (Concat) test set, the enrolled system cuts WER to 32.7% versus 41.0% for the original Personal VAD, mostly on insertion errors from side-talk; the enrollment-less variant reaches 7.0% WER on regular voice-search queries, on par with the non-personalized baseline. Trained on 2.6M utterances (~1,600 hours, 6,923 speakers) plus 35M English audio-text pairs for the enrollment-less path; tested on 194,890 utterances from 1,241 speakers. A downstream-WER metric, not directly comparable to any EER figure elsewhere on this page.
systems.languages_note: English, per the enrollment-less training corpus and test set description.
systems.verification_note: Read in full via an ar5iv HTML mirror of the arXiv source (2204.03793), including the exact Table 2 WER figures and dataset sizes.

systems.name: Selective Attention System (SAS)
systems.licence: Not established from the sources reviewed
systems.task: Binary device-addressed confidence score per utterance, consumed as a routing gate before STT — forward or discard.
systems.availability: Hosted/SDK offering (attenlabs/saa-sdk); the model, weights and inference run server-side over a WebSocket.
systems.best_for: The clearest published statement of device-addressed detection as a routing problem that sits before ASR rather than after it.
systems.watch: Hosted and SDK-only, so despite being the most on-target published system here there is nothing to download and run locally. Its own paper notes a direct F1 comparison against wake-word detection is impossible, because the evaluation corpus was collected with no wake-word protocol in the ground truth.
systems.standout: Positions addressee detection as a structural sibling of wake-word detection rather than a replacement — any device-directed speech as the trigger instead of a fixed phrase, with a tunable threshold in place of phonetic-similarity false accepts.
systems.architecture: Learned classifier sitting after an external VAD, which supplies the speech/non-speech segmentation.
systems.latency_note: Under 150 ms end-to-end at threshold 0.70, per the paper.
systems.accuracy_note: F1 0.86 (precision 0.89, recall 0.83) on the paper's own held-out 60-hour multi-speaker English test set, audio-only configuration at threshold 0.70. Not comparable to any other row on this page.
systems.verification_note: Read against the paper in the governed Imprynt research corpus, pages 4-5 and 13, including the Table 9 wake-word comparison.

systems.name: Streaming On-Device DDSD from Voice and Touch-Based Invocation (Apple)
systems.task: Streaming binary device-directed classification unified across BOTH voice-trigger and touch-button invocation in one model, via a temporal convolutional network (TCN) decision layer over acoustic features, in place of a separate model per invocation type.
systems.availability: No released weights or code — a research paper only, evaluated on in-house test sets.
systems.best_for: The first published streaming model that handles voice-trigger and touch-invoked speech with ONE architecture instead of two, which matters for any system that supports both a wake word and a push-to-talk button.
systems.watch: In-house test sets only, no public benchmark, and no released model. Touch-based EER (~10%) is roughly 3x worse than voice-trigger EER (~3%) in this paper's own numbers — touch invocation is the harder addressee problem, not the easier one intuition suggests.
systems.standout: On the harder touch-invoked task the streaming TCN is statistically tied with a non-streaming upper-bound baseline (9.7% vs 9.6% EER) — unifying invocation types and going streaming cost almost nothing in accuracy there, though the voice-trigger task shows a real streaming penalty (3.1% vs 2.0%).
systems.architecture: Streaming TCN decision layer over acoustic false-trigger-mitigation features, compared against streaming LSTM and non-streaming attention-pooling baselines.
systems.accuracy_note: Voice-trigger set (7.3k utterances, 7:1 directed:undirected): TCN reaches 6.4% FAR at 1% FRR (3.1% EER), against 2.0% EER for a non-streaming attention-pooling upper bound. Touch-based set (38k utterances, 3:1): TCN reaches 25.1% FAR at 3% FRR (9.7% EER), comparable to the 9.6% EER non-streaming upper bound — i.e. streaming costs almost nothing on the harder, touch-invoked task. Both are the paper's own in-house sets; not comparable to any other row here.
systems.training_data: ~150k true and ~30k negative triggers per invocation type, in-house.
systems.verification_note: Read in full via arXiv HTML primary source (arxiv.org/html/2110.04656), including the exact FAR/EER table.

systems.name: Conversational RuBERT (Competitive Interruption Detection)
systems.licence: Not established from the sources reviewed
systems.price_note: Not applicable — research code, not a product
systems.task: Binary text classification of a single successful speech overlap (lasting at least one second) in an ASR-transcribed call-centre dialogue as competitive (floor-claiming, intrusive) or non-competitive (backchannels, simultaneous starts, and other supportive overlap) — a post-hoc classifier run on transcripts, not a real-time audio model.
systems.availability: Training and evaluation code is public on GitHub (gal-dmitry/INTERRUPTION_DETECTION_PUBLIC). The in-house training dataset and the fine-tuned checkpoint are not released — the paper states the dataset "cannot be shared due to privacy issues." Reproducing the classifier requires labelling your own overlap corpus.
systems.best_for: The clearest published demonstration that floor-intent is learnable from text alone, for teams that already have ASR transcripts and no audio pipeline to attach a classifier to.
systems.watch: No fine-tuned checkpoint or training data ships, only the code. It also only scores overlaps that lasted at least a second and succeeded in taking the turn, which is a narrower net than "any overlap" — the short interjections that most need separating from backchannels are exactly what gets filtered out before the classifier ever sees them.
systems.standout: Ablates the framing before the model — shows that including the INTERRUPTED speaker's context (not just the interrupter's) buys most of the accuracy, and that widening the context window past the immediate turns actively hurts performance.
systems.architecture: Conversational RuBERT (DeepPavlov) fine-tuned for binary sequence classification over the interrupter's and interrupted speaker's transcript spans.
systems.input_features: ASR transcript text of both speakers' turns around the overlap. Audio is not used.
systems.accuracy_note: F1-macro 0.8404 (best configuration, using both speakers' context) on the held-out 10th fold of a nine-fold cross-validation, over the authors' private dataset of Russian ASR-transcribed call-centre dialogues — 1,232 competitive and 943 non-competitive labelled overlaps after filtering to successful, 1s+ overlaps (a further 546 were marked undefined by annotators and dropped). Not comparable to any audio-based row on this page, and not independently reproduced.
systems.languages_note: Russian only. The architecture is not language-specific but no other-language checkpoint exists.
systems.verification_note: Read against the full PDF (arxiv.org/pdf/2407.14940) — task and filtering definition (Sec. 3.2), class-distribution tables (Tables 1-2), the F1-macro 0.8404 result (Sec. 4, Table 3), and the public-code/private-data statement under "Availability of Data and Materials."

systems.name: Krisp Interrupt Prediction v1
systems.task: Audio-only 0-1 confidence separating a genuine floor-claiming interruption from a backchannel such as "yeah" or "mm-hmm" while the agent is speaking.
systems.availability: Closed, SDK-only through the paid Krisp VIVA SDK. No open weights.
systems.best_for: The only shipping product that treats backchannel-versus-interruption as its own classification problem rather than a side effect of VAD thresholds.
systems.watch: Closed SDK, English only, and every figure is vendor-reported on a vendor test set. A patent has been filed. Do not confuse with Krisp Turn Prediction v3, which answers end-of-turn and belongs in the Turns section.
systems.standout: Vendor reports a plain VAD baseline fires on almost two thirds of backchannels — the number that makes this a distinct model rather than a tuning knob.
systems.latency_note: Runs on CPU. Mean interruption time 0.833 s at the vendor's recommended threshold of 0.4.
systems.accuracy_note: Balanced accuracy 0.906, F1 0.871, under 6% false-positive rate at threshold 0.4 on the vendor's own 1,721-segment set (1,182 backchannel, 539 interruption). Falls under 3% FPR at threshold 0.7. Vendor-reported, not independently reproduced.

systems.name: LLM Interruption Intent Classifier (JHU / Cao et al.)
systems.licence: Not established from the sources reviewed
systems.price_note: Not applicable — research code; the classifier itself runs as pay-per-token OpenAI GPT-4o-mini API usage, not a separately priced product.
systems.task: Four-way classification of interrupter intent — cooperative agreement, cooperative assistance, cooperative clarification, or disruptive — applied to the transcript of overlapping user speech while the robot is talking, to decide whether to yield the floor or continue.
systems.availability: Integration and prompting code is public on GitHub (intuitivecomputing/interruption-handling-system). The classifier itself is a prompted call to OpenAI's proprietary GPT-4o-mini, not a locally-run or downloadable model. Two hard-coded shortcuts bypass it entirely — a detected wakeword is always treated as disruptive, and any overlap with under 2 seconds of planned robot speech remaining skips classification.
systems.best_for: The only candidate found here validated live inside a running dialogue system with real users rather than on a static corpus, and the most explicit that its classifier is a thin wrapper around a general-purpose LLM rather than a purpose-built model.
systems.watch: The classifier is GPT-4o-mini prompted per interruption, not a released model — every deployment pays OpenAI's API cost and latency, and behaviour can drift if OpenAI changes what sits behind that model name. Per-class counts are small (2 examples of cooperative assistance in the whole study), so only the disruptive / cooperative-agreement split is well-supported. It also demonstrates this category's blind spot from the inside: the system's own authors did not trust the LLM classifier alone for the highest-stakes cases, and hard-coded two bypasses (wakeword, <2s-remaining) around it instead.
systems.standout: Two of its four classes carry actual content rather than a bare acknowledgment — "cooperative clarification" (a question) and "cooperative assistance" (a suggestion) — which Krisp's binary framing collapses into a single "not floor-claiming" bucket; the paper's own error analysis shows these content-bearing cooperative classes get misclassified as disruptive more often than plain backchannels do.
systems.architecture: Prompt-engineered GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI), called per-interruption on the ASR transcript plus dialogue context. No locally trained model.
systems.input_features: ASR transcript of the overlapping user speech plus dialogue context. Audio is not used by the classifier itself.
systems.accuracy_note: 88.78% of interruptions correctly classified (87 of 98) in a live user study — 21 participants, 111 system-handled interruptions out of 121 total user-initiated interruptions observed across 206.59 minutes of interaction with an LLM-powered social robot. Of the subset that actually reached the intent-classifier module (55, after excluding the wakeword and under-2-second shortcuts), 80.00% were classified correctly. The most common true class was disruptive (76.03% of coded interruptions); cooperative assistance had only 2 examples in the entire study. This is the paper's own study, not independently reproduced.
systems.verification_note: Read against the full PDF (arxiv.org/pdf/2501.01568) — GPT-4o-mini prompting design (Sec. III-IV), the wakeword/2-second bypass rules (Sec. VI.B), the 88.78%/80.00% results with their n counts (Sec. VI.A-VI.C, Table I-II), and the "Code:" availability line pointing at the GitHub repository.

systems.name: pyannote overlapped-speech-detection
systems.task: Frame-level detection of regions where two or more speakers are talking at once.
systems.availability: Weights on Hugging Face, behind a gated accept-conditions form.
systems.best_for: Flagging that overlap is happening at all, as an input to whatever decides what the overlap means.
systems.watch: Detects that overlap occurred, never what it meant — a backchannel and a barge-in are identical to this model. Gated on Hugging Face, so a build needs an accepted licence and a token.
systems.standout: One of very few permissively licensed, downloadable models on this page that addresses overlap directly rather than as a by-product of diarization.
systems.architecture: Segmentation model, sibling of pyannote segmentation-3.0

systems.name: Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST)
systems.licence: BSD-3-Clause (repo LICENSE covers the source tree; no separate statement was found for the pretrained checkpoints specifically)
systems.task: Multi-label tagging over AudioSet's 527 classes from a sequence of spectrogram patches, via a convolution-free attention-only transformer.
systems.availability: Multiple pretrained checkpoints (tiny224/small224/base224/base384) published as direct Dropbox downloads from the repo.
systems.best_for: A well-documented transformer baseline when CNN taggers like PANNs plateau and you want the accuracy headroom a bigger attention model buys.
systems.watch: The repo has had no commits since May 2023, and the LICENSE file only addresses the code — the checkpoint weights are not separately licensed, so a shipper is relying on the code licence covering the artefact too, not a written statement that it does.
systems.standout: The first fully convolution-free audio tagger to match/beat CNN baselines on AudioSet — since superseded in raw mAP by BEATs and PaSST.
systems.architecture: Vision-Transformer-style patch embedding over a log-Mel spectrogram, initialised from an ImageNet-pretrained ViT
systems.accuracy_note: mAP 0.459 (single model, weight-averaged) on AudioSet's full evaluation set, rising to 0.485 with a multi-model ensemble — the repo's own reported figures, standard 16 kHz AudioSet protocol.
systems.verification_note: LICENSE and README read directly from the repo; pushed_at=2023-05-21 via GitHub API, read 2026-08-19.

systems.name: BEATs
systems.licence: MIT (unilm repository licence; the BEATs subproject states no additional restriction beyond it)
systems.task: Multi-label tagging over AudioSet's 527 classes, from a model pretrained with a self-distilled discrete acoustic tokenizer rather than a fixed spectrogram target.
systems.availability: Multiple checkpoint generations (iter1 through iter3+, tokenizer and fine-tuned variants, AS20K and AS2M) published via OneDrive links in the repo README.
systems.best_for: The strongest openly-checkpointed AudioSet mAP on this page when accuracy matters more than inference cost.
systems.watch: Distributed inside the large microsoft/unilm monorepo, whose top-level MIT licence the BEATs page inherits without a subproject-specific restatement — worth a second look before treating that as settled for a Microsoft Research release. Params/model size are not printed in the README text (only in result-table images), so no figure is given here.
systems.standout: Learns its own pretraining targets (a self-distilled tokenizer) instead of a fixed spectrogram reconstruction loss, which is what let later iterations keep improving on the same architecture.
systems.accuracy_note: mAP 0.506 on AudioSet-2M for audio-only models using no external data — the paper's own headline SOTA claim (best iteration; per-iteration breakdown is in README chart images, not extracted here to avoid quoting a number the source did not print as text).
systems.verification_note: README and LICENSE read via GitHub; abstract mAP figure cross-checked against the arXiv abstract (2212.09058). pushed_at=2026-01-23 for microsoft/unilm as a whole (monorepo — not specific evidence of BEATs subfolder activity), read 2026-08-19.

systems.name: CED (Consistent Ensemble Distillation)
systems.licence: GPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE; applies to code and the published checkpoints together, no split)
systems.task: Multi-label tagging over AudioSet's 527 classes, at four ensemble-distilled size tiers (Tiny/Mini/Small/Base).
systems.availability: All four checkpoints on Zenodo and on Hugging Face (mispeech/ced-tiny through mispeech/ced-base); a Hugging Face Spaces demo exists for CED-Base.
systems.best_for: A size/accuracy ladder in one family, so a deployment can pick the smallest tier that clears its accuracy bar instead of committing to one model size up front.
systems.watch: GPL-3.0, not a permissive licence — shipping CED inside a closed-source product carries GPL's copyleft obligations, unlike every Apache/MIT/BSD row on this page. Read that before assuming "open weights" means "safe to embed."
systems.accuracy_note: AudioSet-2M mAP by tier, per the repo's own table: Tiny 0.481, Mini 0.490, Small 0.496, Base 0.500. All four figures use the same AS-2M evaluation protocol, so the tiers are directly comparable to each other (but not to a different paper's AudioSet split).
systems.verification_note: LICENSE and README/table read from the repo; pushed_at=2026-03-20 via GitHub API, read 2026-08-19.

systems.name: ConvNeXt-Tiny for AudioSet
systems.task: Multi-label tagging over AudioSet's 527 classes, via an image-model ConvNeXt-Tiny backbone adapted to log-Mel spectrograms.
systems.availability: Two ConvNeXt-Tiny checkpoints on Zenodo (convnext_tiny_471mAP.pth and a variant with AudioCaps files stripped from training); pip-installable inference package from the repo.
systems.best_for: A CNN alternative to PANNs that trades roughly a third of the parameters for comparable-or-better mAP, when model size on a small device is the binding constraint.
systems.watch: A research-scale release from a single academic author, not a vendor — no SLA, and the repo has had no commits since February 2025.
systems.standout: Matches or beats several larger audio transformers at 28M parameters by reusing an image-classification backbone rather than a bespoke audio architecture.
systems.architecture: ConvNeXt-Tiny (an image-classification CNN family) over a log-Mel spectrogram, via torchlibrosa — same front end as PANNs
systems.accuracy_note: mAP 0.471 on the AudioSet evaluation test subset (1,921,982 training files), per the paper (Interspeech 2023) and repo.
systems.verification_note: Repo, README and LICENSE read directly; params count taken verbatim from the repo's own printed value. pushed_at=2025-02-19 via GitHub API, read 2026-08-19.

systems.name: HTS-AT (Hierarchical Token-Semantic Audio Transformer)
systems.task: Multi-label tagging over AudioSet's 527 classes, plus frame-level sound event detection (WHEN a class occurs, not just whether it does) via a token-semantic module on the same backbone.
systems.availability: Pretrained checkpoints for AudioSet, ESC-50, Speech Commands v2 and DESED published via a Google Drive link in the repo.
systems.best_for: The only row on this page that both tags a clip AND localises when each event occurred, in one model, at a third the parameters of AST.
systems.watch: The repo's own README and the paper abstract both assert "new SOTA on AudioSet" without printing the exact mAP figure as text — it appears only in result-table images. No accuracy figure is given here rather than transcribe one from an image and risk a misread digit.
systems.standout: The token-semantic module reframes the same classification backbone as a detector, so a single 30M-parameter model does the job PANNs/AST/BEATs each need a separate detection head for.
systems.architecture: Swin-Transformer-style hierarchical windowed attention over a spectrogram, plus a token-semantic head for localisation
systems.verification_note: README, LICENSE and arXiv abstract (2202.00874) all read directly; the abstract does not state a numeric mAP either. pushed_at=2025-09-18 via GitHub API, read 2026-08-19.

systems.name: LAION CLAP
systems.licence: Code CC0-1.0 (public domain, per the GitHub repo); the released checkpoints' own Hugging Face model card (laion/clap-htsat-fused) states Apache-2.0 — the two statements do not contradict each other, but note they are not the same document.
systems.task: Zero-shot classification against ARBITRARY text prompts, via cosine similarity between an audio embedding and a text embedding — not a fixed 527-class label set, the structurally distinct approach on this page.
systems.availability: Multiple checkpoints on Hugging Face (general-purpose, music, speech, and fused variants); default release is 630k-audioset-best.pt.
systems.best_for: The one row here that answers "does this clip match this arbitrary description" instead of "which of these fixed 527 labels applies" — useful when the ontology you actually care about is not AudioSet's.
systems.watch: Zero-shot text-prompt classification is measurably less accurate than a tuned fixed-label classifier at any given label; ESC-50's 50 classes are a much coarser ontology than AudioSet's 527, so the reported accuracy figure is answering an easier question than PANNs/AST/BEATs/CED are.
systems.standout: Genuinely open-vocabulary — a new sound category is a new text prompt, not a new training run, which none of the fixed-label taggers on this page can offer.
systems.params: ~0.2B (HTSAT-base audio encoder + text encoder combined, per the Hugging Face model card)
systems.architecture: Contrastive dual-encoder (audio tower + text tower), audio side built on an HTSAT backbone
systems.accuracy_note: Zero-shot accuracy up to 90.14%% on ESC-50 (a 50-class environmental-sound benchmark, not AudioSet) for the music-specialised variant, per the repo's reported figures. ESC-50 accuracy and AudioSet mAP are different tasks on different label sets — do not read this figure against the AudioSet mAP numbers elsewhere on this page.
systems.training_data: LAION-Audio-630K audio-caption pairs, extended with AudioSet, music and speech data in the larger checkpoints (~4M samples)
systems.verification_note: Repo and Hugging Face model card both read directly. pushed_at=2025-05-15 via GitHub API, read 2026-08-19 (~15 months stale).

systems.name: M2D (Masked Modeling Duo) / M2D-AS / M2D-CLAP
systems.licence: NTT "Software License Agreement for Evaluation" (proprietary; not open source). Grants a royalty-free licence for internal, NON-COMMERCIAL evaluation only; explicitly forbids redistribution, sublicensing, and modification/reverse-engineering, and NTT may remotely disable the software.
systems.price_note: No monetary cost, but licensed for non-commercial evaluation only — there is no published path to commercial or production use.
systems.task: Multi-label tagging over AudioSet's 527 classes (the M2D-AS variant), or joint audio-text embedding for zero-shot classification (M2D-CLAP) — both built on the same masked-modelling pretraining framework.
systems.availability: Multiple checkpoints via GitHub releases (M2D-CLAP_2025 is the vendor's recommended default; M2D-AS is the AudioSet-specialised variant).
systems.best_for: Nothing this page can recommend for actual deployment — its mAP is competitive, but the licence forecloses that use before accuracy is even a question.
systems.watch: This is the licence-catch the section exists to name: the repo reads like every other open research release on this page — MIT-style README, pip installable, GitHub-hosted — but the LICENSE.pdf is a proprietary NTT evaluation agreement that forbids redistribution and commercial use outright and lets NTT remotely disable the software. Confirmed by reading the PDF directly, not inferred from the repo's tone.
systems.standout: Its 2025 checkpoint's reported AudioSet-2M mAP (0.490) sits within a point of BEATs' state-of-the-art figure, on paper the strongest recent open-CHECKPOINT tagger here — undercut entirely by what "open" means below.
systems.architecture: ViT-Base-scale dual masked-modelling encoder (student/teacher), log-Mel spectrogram input via torchlibrosa (same front end as PANNs)
systems.accuracy_note: mAP 0.490 on AudioSet-2M evaluation for M2D-CLAP_2025 (the vendor-recommended checkpoint), 0.485 for the fine-tuned M2D-CLAP_2024 — both per the repo's own reported table, standard AS-2M protocol.
systems.verification_note: LICENSE.pdf downloaded and read verbatim (Software License Agreement for Evaluation, NTT); README read for architecture/accuracy claims. pushed_at=2026-02-23 via GitHub API, read 2026-08-19.

systems.name: PANNs (CNN14)
systems.task: Multi-label tagging over AudioSet's 527 sound-event classes, including speech, television and music — the classes that separate incidental background audio from a person addressing the system.
systems.availability: Pretrained checkpoints published, including a Cnn14_16k variant matching a 16 kHz pipeline.
systems.best_for: A well-understood, permissively licensed baseline for deciding whether the sound in the room is speech, a television, or something else entirely.
systems.watch: AudioSet labels are weak and YouTube-sourced, and mAP over 527 classes does not transfer to a five-class conversational ontology. It answers what the sound is, never who it was addressed to.
systems.standout: The MobileNetV1 variant reaches mAP 0.389 at roughly 8.6% of CNN14's parameters and multiply-adds, which makes the accuracy-for-size trade explicit rather than something you have to discover.
systems.architecture: Large-kernel CNN over log-Mel, pretrained on AudioSet
systems.accuracy_note: mAP 0.431 on the AudioSet evaluation set, against the 0.314 of Google's original baseline. An audio-tagging metric over 527 classes; it says nothing about conversational-role accuracy.

systems.name: PaSST (Patchout faSt Spectrogram Transformer)
systems.task: Multi-label tagging over AudioSet's 527 classes, via a spectrogram transformer trained with structured "patchout" (dropping time/frequency patches during training) to cut compute.
systems.availability: Multiple pretrained checkpoints via the repo's releases page, loadable through a `get_model()` helper.
systems.best_for: A transformer tagger that was built explicitly to cut the training cost that makes AST-style models expensive to retrain on a custom ontology.
systems.watch: No commits since January 2024; params/model size are not stated as plain text in the README (only encoded in checkpoint filenames), so no figure is given here.
systems.standout: Patchout is a training-time technique, not an inference-time one — the accuracy gain comes from what it lets a from-scratch retrain afford, which matters if the plan is to fine-tune rather than use the stock checkpoint.
systems.accuracy_note: mAP 0.476 for the single best-reported checkpoint (passt_s_swa_p16_128_ap476), rising to 0.4956 for a large ensemble — both per the repo's own documented AudioSet results.
systems.verification_note: README and LICENSE read directly from the repo. pushed_at=2024-01-12 via GitHub API, read 2026-08-19.

systems.name: YAMNet
systems.licence: Apache-2.0 (confirmed in the source file headers; code and checkpoint ship from the same repo under the same licence)
systems.task: Multi-label tagging over 521 of AudioSet's 527 sound-event classes, one label set per 0.96 s input frame.
systems.availability: Pretrained checkpoint published directly in the repo (also mirrored on TF-Hub/Kaggle); loads with stock TensorFlow, no training required.
systems.best_for: The lowest-friction way to get a "speech / music / TV / dog / door" read on incidental audio — tiny, Apache-licensed, and available since 2019.
systems.watch: 521 of AudioSet's 527 classes, not all of them — its own class map omits six. Trained on weakly-labelled YouTube audio like every AudioSet model here, and its balanced-subset mAP is not comparable to a full-eval-set figure.
systems.standout: At 3.7M parameters it is an order of magnitude smaller than every transformer tagger on this page, and still clears a documented mAP baseline.
systems.architecture: MobileNetV1 depthwise-separable CNN over a 64-bin log-Mel spectrogram (16 kHz mono input, 125-7500 Hz mel range)
systems.accuracy_note: Balanced mAP 0.306 on AudioSet's balanced evaluation subset, per the model's own README — a different eval protocol and denominator than the full-evaluation-set mAP figures quoted elsewhere on this page, not directly comparable to them.
systems.verification_note: README fetched from the repo; Apache-2.0 confirmed via file headers across yamnet.py/params.py/inference.py/features.py. Repo-level `pushed_at` is current (it is a live monorepo), but that reflects tensorflow/models as a whole, not evidence the yamnet subfolder itself has changed recently — status called dormant on that basis.

systems.name: AASIST
systems.task: Binary synthetic-vs-genuine (bona fide) confidence score for automatic-speaker-verification anti-spoofing / audio deepfake detection.
systems.availability: Official PyTorch implementation with pretrained AASIST and AASIST-L checkpoints on GitHub.
systems.best_for: A strong, permissively licensed, downloadable baseline for the specific question "is this a synthetic voice" -- the standard reference point most later spoofing-countermeasure papers compare against.
systems.watch: Trained and evaluated entirely on ASVspoof 2019 LA -- a curated benchmark of known TTS/voice-conversion attack types. Countermeasures in this lineage generalise poorly to unseen synthesis methods and real-world audio; published replications training an AASIST-family model on ASVspoof 2021 and evaluating cross-dataset on the In-the-Wild set report EER climbing from well under 1% in-domain into the high twenties. Treat 0.83% as a ceiling measured on one specific benchmark, not a real-world detection rate.
systems.standout: Both a full-size and an ~85K-parameter lightweight (AASIST-L) checkpoint ship from the same repo, so the size/accuracy trade is explicit rather than something you have to infer.
systems.params: AASIST-L: 85.3k (85,306 parameters). Full AASIST's parameter count is not disclosed in the repo's own documentation.
systems.architecture: Integrated spectro-temporal graph attention network operating end-to-end on raw waveform -- no handcrafted features.
systems.accuracy_note: EER 0.83% / min t-DCF 0.0275 on the ASVspoof 2019 Logical Access evaluation set for AASIST; EER 0.99% / min t-DCF 0.0309 for the lightweight AASIST-L -- both the paper's own in-domain figures.
systems.verification_note: Licence, parameter count and EER figures read directly from the GitHub README. The cross-dataset generalisation claim is sourced to published replications surveying the lineage (e.g. arXiv 2603.05852, "How Well Do Current Speech Deepfake Detection Methods Generalize to the Real World?"), not to the AASIST paper itself, which reports only in-domain numbers.

systems.name: audEERING wav2vec2-large-robust-12-ft-emotion-msp-dim
systems.licence: CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 (research use; a separate commercial licence is available directly from audEERING)
systems.price_note: Free for research use under CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0; commercial licence terms and pricing are negotiated directly with audEERING and are not published.
systems.task: Continuous 3-dimensional regression -- arousal, dominance, valence, each roughly 0-1 -- per utterance, rather than a categorical emotion label.
systems.availability: Weights on Hugging Face; an ONNX export is also published via Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.6221127).
systems.best_for: The one row here trained on genuinely spontaneous emotional speech rather than an acted corpus, and the only one outputting continuous arousal/valence/dominance instead of a fixed label set -- useful when "how activated, positive, and in-control did this sound" is a better fit than a discrete emotion tag.
systems.watch: Downloadable weights with no API gate read as an open, self-hostable checkpoint at a glance, but the licence is CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 -- research use only. A commercial deployment needs a separate negotiated licence from audEERING, and no price for that is published anywhere in the sources reviewed.
systems.standout: Fine-tuned and evaluated on MSP-Podcast, a naturalistic corpus built by retrieving emotional speech from real podcasts -- the direct answer to IEMOCAP's acted-speech caveat that applies to two other rows on this page.
systems.params: ~200M (Wav2Vec2-Large-Robust backbone, pruned from 24 to 12 transformer layers before fine-tuning)
systems.architecture: Wav2Vec2-Large-Robust backbone pruned to 12 layers, fine-tuned end-to-end for dimensional affect regression.
systems.accuracy_note: Valence CCC (concordance correlation coefficient) .638 on the MSP-Podcast test set, per the paper's own headline figure (Wagner et al., "Dawn of the Transformer Era in Speech Emotion Recognition," arXiv 2203.07378). Arousal and dominance CCC for this specific 12-layer checkpoint were not confirmed from the sources reviewed.
systems.training_data: Fine-tuned on MSP-Podcast v1.7 -- naturalistic speech retrieved and segmented from real podcast recordings, not an acted corpus.
systems.runs_on: CPU or GPU -- the model card documents `device_map="auto"`, implying CPU inference is supported though not benchmarked for latency.
systems.released: 2022 (paper); checkpoint hosted on Hugging Face since 2022-04-06
systems.verification_note: Licence and architecture read directly from the Hugging Face model card; CCC figure read from the paper abstract (arXiv 2203.07378).

systems.name: emotion2vec
systems.licence: Code MIT (GitHub repo). Hugging Face weights are tagged license: other / model-license, linking to the FunASR GitHub repo rather than a separate model-weights licence file.
systems.task: Self-supervised utterance- and frame-level (50 Hz) speech-emotion representation, evaluated in the paper via a linear probe into categorical emotion (4-class IEMOCAP probe in the headline result; the plus family ships a 9-class probe -- angry, disgusted, fearful, happy, neutral, other, sad, surprised, unknown).
systems.availability: Code and checkpoints (base, base_finetuned, plus-seed, plus-base, plus-large) on GitHub, Hugging Face and ModelScope.
systems.best_for: A ready categorical (or, via the plus family, more granular) emotion signal without training your own head -- the plus-large checkpoint posts the highest reported IEMOCAP number of any open self-supervised model in its own paper's comparison table.
systems.watch: IEMOCAP is a scripted-and-improvised ACTED corpus recorded by ten actors in a lab -- the 71.79% figure will not hold on spontaneous, in-the-wild speech, and the paper does not report a naturalistic-corpus number for direct comparison. Separately, the Hugging Face weights carry a licence tag of `other` pointing at the FunASR code repository rather than a dedicated model-weights licence file -- confirm terms with Alibaba/DAMO before a commercial deployment, since a repo's code licence and its published model-weights terms are not guaranteed to match.
systems.standout: Ships three plus-family sizes (seed/base/large) explicitly trading model size against label-noise robustness on pseudo-labelled data, so the size-vs-robustness trade is documented rather than left to be discovered.
systems.params: ~90M (emotion2vec+ base) to ~300M (emotion2vec+ large); the original emotion2vec checkpoint is smaller than either.
systems.architecture: data2vec-style self-supervised representation learning specialised for emotion, with iterative pseudo-labelling used to scale the plus family's training data.
systems.accuracy_note: 71.79% weighted accuracy on IEMOCAP under the SUPERB protocol (frozen backbone, linear-probe downstream head, standard splits) -- the paper's own headline figure, ahead of the next-best self-supervised model in the same comparison table (Vesper-12 at 70.70%).
systems.training_data: emotion2vec+ large: ~42,500 hours of large-scale pseudo-labelled speech, filtered down from a 160,000-hour pool.
systems.languages_note: Claims robustness across Mandarin, English, French, German and Italian per the project README; no per-language breakdown found.
systems.verification_note: IEMOCAP figure read from the paper's own comparison table (arXiv 2312.15185) via search excerpt; licence tag read directly from the Hugging Face model card YAML front-matter (emotion2vec/emotion2vec_plus_large).

systems.name: Krisp VIVA 2.0 Signal Detectors
systems.price_note: Bundled into existing VIVA SDK pricing at no additional charge, per the launch announcement; VIVA itself is a paid commercial SDK licence.
systems.task: Three real-time, audio-only classifiers bundled together -- synthetic speech (TTS) detection (binary genuine-vs-generated, aimed at recognising when an inbound call is answered by another voice-AI agent or IVR rather than a human), speaker gender classification, and speaker accent classification used to route audio to the best-matched STT model.
systems.availability: Closed, SDK-only through the paid Krisp VIVA 2.0 SDK. No open weights, no standalone model access outside the SDK.
systems.best_for: The one shipping product bundling synthetic-speech detection with gender and accent classification as real-time, CPU-only signals for a live voice-agent pipeline -- genuinely on-target for this category, if living inside the SDK is acceptable.
systems.watch: Closed SDK with no published accuracy or latency figures for any of the three detectors as of the launch announcement (2026-05-06) -- contrast with this same vendor's own Interrupt Prediction v1 (see the floor-intent category on this page), which does publish a held-out-set F1. No dataset size, evaluation set, or per-class breakdown is disclosed for the Synthetic Speech, Gender or Accent detectors, so none of the three can currently be verified from public sources -- treat this row as a vendor capability claim, not a measured one.
systems.standout: Reads all three signals -- synthetic speech, gender, accent -- from audio alone with no transcription step, and feeds the accent signal directly into STT model selection rather than treating it as a side classification with no consumer.
systems.runs_on: Standard server CPU, per the vendor -- no GPU required.
systems.verification_note: Confirmed the three detectors exist and their stated function from the Krisp VIVA 2.0 launch blog post (krisp.ai/blog/viva-2-0-ai-infrastructure-for-voice-ai-agents) and the corroborating Businesswire release; no independent accuracy, latency or dataset evidence was found for any of the three.

systems.name: SpeechBrain emotion-recognition-wav2vec2-IEMOCAP
systems.task: 4-class categorical emotion classification (neutral, happy, sad, angry) from a single utterance -- a complete fine-tuned classifier, not an embedding needing a downstream head.
systems.availability: Weights on Hugging Face, loadable directly through SpeechBrain's EncoderClassifier interface.
systems.best_for: The simplest downloadable categorical emotion classifier to drop into a pipeline -- permissive licence, small footprint, runs on CPU, no separate head to train.
systems.watch: IEMOCAP is acted speech (professional/semi-professional actors, scripted and improvised scenes recorded in a lab) -- the model card itself declines to warrant performance on any other dataset. Four emotion classes is also a coarse ontology next to emotion2vec's 9-class label set.
systems.standout: One of very few rows on this page shipped as a complete fine-tuned classifier rather than an embedding that still needs a task-specific head.
systems.architecture: wav2vec2-base fine-tuned end-to-end (not a frozen-backbone linear probe) on IEMOCAP.
systems.accuracy_note: 78.7% accuracy (75.3% average across folds) on the IEMOCAP test split, per the model card's own reported figure.
systems.runs_on: CPU or GPU -- the model card documents GPU as optional (`run_opts={"device":"cuda"}`), not required.
systems.verification_note: Licence, task and accuracy figure read directly from the Hugging Face model card.

systems.name: TRILLsson
systems.task: Fixed-length utterance embedding (a family of checkpoints from 22 MB to 314 MB) for downstream paralinguistic classifiers -- emotion, speaker traits, dysarthria, synthetic-vs-real and other non-semantic speech tasks. Not itself a classifier; nothing here decides anything on its own.
systems.availability: Checkpoints published on Kaggle Models (migrated from TensorFlow Hub in 2023, tfhub.dev links now redirect) across the full distilled size range.
systems.best_for: The reference general-purpose paralinguistic embedding -- reach for this when you need one small, frozen encoder to feed several downstream classifiers (emotion, synthetic-speech, speaker traits) instead of training a separate front-end for each.
systems.watch: This is an embedding, not a classifier -- a task-specific head (even a linear probe) has to be trained on top of it before it answers anything. Hosting moved from TensorFlow Hub to Kaggle Models in 2023; treat any tfhub.dev link you find elsewhere as stale.
systems.standout: Explicitly a distillation product -- the paper reports the accuracy-for-size trade across a whole family of checkpoints rather than shipping one size and leaving you to guess what a smaller one costs.
systems.params: 5.0M (TRILLsson 1) to 88.6M (TRILLsson 5), per the paper's own Table 3
systems.architecture: Knowledge-distilled from a large paralinguistic teacher (CAP12/TRILL lineage) onto smaller student encoders, aimed specifically at devices where the teacher's footprint is impractical.
systems.accuracy_note: On the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark suite, the largest distilled checkpoint retains over 96% of the teacher's accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks; even the smallest (22 MB) checkpoint retains over 90% on 6 of 7 tasks. Both outperform an open Wav2Vec 2.0 baseline on 6 of 7 tasks, per the paper's own comparison table.
systems.verification_note: Read against the paper abstract (arXiv 2203.00236) and the current Kaggle Models hosting page for google/trillsson. Parameter counts (5.0M-88.6M) read from the paper's own Table 3, which reports both Params (M) and Size (MB) per named variant (TRILLsson 1 through 5) -- distinct from the file-size figures already used above.

systems.name: WavLM Base+ (frozen paralinguistic backbone)
systems.task: No classifier output on its own -- a frozen self-supervised speech encoder whose layer-wise hidden states (via a learned weighted sum, not the raw final layer) are the standard SUPERB-benchmark input for downstream paralinguistic heads, emotion recognition among them.
systems.availability: Pretrained checkpoint on Hugging Face (microsoft/wavlm-base-plus) -- NOT fine-tuned for any downstream task, and a different checkpoint from the SV-finetuned WavLM-Base-Plus-SV already listed in Speakerid.
systems.best_for: The shared frozen front-end when WavLM already sits elsewhere in the pipeline (ASR, diarization) and you want a paralinguistic head to tap the same encoder rather than adding a second one -- the SUPERB weighted-layer-sum protocol this checkpoint is benchmarked under.
systems.watch: Ships no classification head of any kind -- attaching one, even a linear probe, is required work. Unlike TRILLsson it was not purpose-built or marketed for paralinguistic tasks specifically -- SUPERB benchmarks it alongside ASR, diarization and speaker verification as one general-purpose backbone, so "paralinguistic" is one use among several rather than the product's stated purpose. The weights are CC-BY-SA-3.0, a share-alike licence -- the identical catch already flagged on WavLM-Base-Plus-SV in the Speakerid section, because it is the same checkpoint family.
systems.standout: The only row here that is neither a shipped classifier nor a distillation product -- it is the backbone most SUPERB-benchmarked emotion heads are actually built on, WavLM's own published SUPERB comparison included.
systems.architecture: Transformer encoder pretrained with masked speech prediction plus a denoising objective (gated relative position bias) on 94k hours of speech -- Libri-Light, GigaSpeech and VoxPopuli.
systems.verification_note: Licence confirmed by fetching github.com/microsoft/UniSpeech/blob/main/LICENSE directly (CC BY-SA 3.0 Unported) -- the same licence already verified for WavLM-Base-Plus-SV in configs/speakerid.yaml. Parameter count and pretraining data read from the WavLM paper (arXiv 2110.13900) and the Hugging Face model card. SUPERB/paralinguistic usage sourced to the SUPERB benchmark's own task suite (which includes Emotion Recognition on IEMOCAP as one of its standard tasks) plus the governed research corpus's WavLM notes (topic 6-pretraining-representations).

systems.name: BC-ResNet
systems.task: No shipped classifier for any task on this page. A reference architecture for small acoustic classification, published against Google Speech Commands, that you instantiate and train on your own ontology.
systems.availability: Official implementation published; the released checkpoints are keyword spotting, not addressee or event classification.
systems.best_for: The strongest size-to-accuracy starting point when you have labelled data and need a classifier small enough to sit on a microcontroller.
systems.watch: This is a backbone, not a classifier — the Speech Commands accuracy says nothing about a conversational ontology, which is substantially more ambiguous than distinguishing isolated words. Parameter count and FLOPs are screening metrics, never latency measurements.
systems.standout: Its published family scales from 9.2k to 54.2k parameters within one architecture, so a size-versus-accuracy sweep does not confound the two.
systems.architecture: Broadcasted residual network — frequency-depthwise processing combined with temporal processing, rather than treating time and frequency identically
systems.accuracy_note: 96.9% on Google Speech Commands v2 for the 9.2k-parameter BC-ResNet-1, in the original paper's own comparison. A twelve-word keyword task; it is an architecture sanity check and nothing more.

systems.name: DS-CNN (Hello Edge)
systems.task: No shipped classifier for any task on this page. A reference architecture for small acoustic classification, published against Google Speech Commands, that you instantiate and train on your own ontology.
systems.availability: Official implementation published (Arm Research); the repository trains and ships example DS-CNN keyword-spotting checkpoints, not any task on this page.
systems.best_for: The reference point for a genuine microcontroller-class budget — sub-500 KB, 8-bit-quantized, with a published memory/accuracy tradeoff curve across three sizes, validated against a real Cortex-M7 deployment.
systems.watch: This is a backbone, not a classifier — the repository trains and evaluates keyword-spotting checkpoints only. The paper's one on-device latency figure is for a different (DNN) model, not DS-CNN itself; do not carry it over. Memory-footprint figures are a screening metric, never a latency measurement.
systems.standout: One of the only rows on this page whose accuracy figures are reported for the actual 8-bit-quantized deployment artefact, rather than float32 accuracy with quantization treated as an afterthought.
systems.model_size: 38.6 KB (DS-CNN S) to 497.6 KB (DS-CNN L), 8-bit-quantized weights and activations
systems.architecture: Depthwise-separable convolutions after an initial standard convolution — the design MobileNet later popularized for images, applied here to spectrograms specifically for a microcontroller memory budget.
systems.latency_note: The paper measures ~12 ms per inference (including MFCC feature extraction) on an STM32F746G-DISCO board (Arm Cortex-M7 @ 216 MHz) — but for its DNN reference model specifically, not for DS-CNN. No DS-CNN latency figure is given; do not substitute the DNN number for it.
systems.accuracy_note: 95.4% on Google Speech Commands v0.01's 12-class task (10 words + unknown + silence) for the largest, 497.6 KB DS-CNN L, per the paper's own Table 5 (arXiv:1711.07128). The smallest, 38.6 KB DS-CNN S, reaches 94.4%. A twelve-word task; says nothing about a conversational ontology.
systems.verification_note: Read against the paper (arXiv:1711.07128, Zhang, Suda, Lai & Chandra, 2017) and the official Apache-2.0 repository, ARM-software/ML-KWS-for-MCU (LICENSE fetched and confirmed).

systems.name: Keyword Transformer (KWT)
systems.task: No shipped classifier for any task on this page. A reference architecture for small acoustic classification, published against Google Speech Commands, that you instantiate and train on your own ontology.
systems.availability: Official implementation published (Arm ML Research); the repository ships pretrained checkpoints for KWT-1/2/3 on Google Speech Commands' 12-label keyword task, not any task on this page.
systems.best_for: The strongest published accuracy on the 12/35-label Speech Commands tasks among backbones on this page, and the one to reach for if attention (rather than convolution) is the axis you want to explore for a small classifier.
systems.watch: This is a backbone, not a classifier — the released checkpoints are keyword-spotting only. Transformers are known to need more data/regularisation than CNNs of similar size; the paper's own knowledge-distillation step exists to compensate for that on the relatively small Speech Commands corpus, which may not hold for a different, larger conversational ontology.
systems.standout: A fully self-attentional design with no convolutional stem at all — unlike every other row here, which is CNN- or CNN-hybrid-based — and it matches or beats them anyway, at parameter counts comparable to res15.
systems.architecture: Pure self-attention transformer (ViT-style) applied to MFCC spectrogram patches split in the TIME domain — the paper found time-domain patches beat frequency-domain ones — with no convolutional stem. Optionally trained with knowledge distillation from an MHAtt-RNN teacher (the KWT-α variants).
systems.input_features: MFCC spectrogram (40 mel-scale bins), partitioned into non-overlapping time-domain patches
systems.latency_note: The paper measures on-device latency on a OnePlus 6 (Snapdragon 845) via TFLite, single-threaded, and finds KWT competitive with DS-CNN, TC-ResNet and MHAtt-RNN at matched accuracy — but reports this only as a plot (its Figure 6), not a table of exact millisecond figures.
systems.accuracy_note: 97.72% (±0.01) on Google Speech Commands V2's 12-label task for the undistilled 607K-parameter KWT-1, rising to 98.54% (±0.17) for the 5.36M-parameter KWT-3, per the paper's own Table 3 (arXiv:2104.00769, three-run 95% CIs). A distilled KWT-3-α variant reaches 98.56% (±0.07). All on a twelve-word task; says nothing about a conversational ontology.
systems.verification_note: Read against the paper (arXiv:2104.00769, Berg, O'Connor & Tairum Cruz, Interspeech 2021) and the official Apache-2.0 repository, ARM-software/keyword-transformer (LICENSE.txt fetched and confirmed).

systems.name: MatchboxNet
systems.licence: Code (NVIDIA NeMo toolkit) is Apache-2.0, confirmed in the repo's own LICENSE file. The officially published Speech Commands checkpoints on NVIDIA NGC are gated separately behind the NGC Terms of Use, a EULA, not Apache-2.0 — read that before assuming the checkpoint inherits the code's licence.
systems.price_note: Free / self-host (code); checkpoints require accepting NGC's Terms of Use
systems.task: No shipped classifier for any task on this page. A reference architecture for small acoustic classification, published against Google Speech Commands, that you instantiate and train on your own ontology.
systems.availability: Official training config published as part of NVIDIA's NeMo toolkit; NVIDIA has also published Speech Commands checkpoints on NGC under NGC's own EULA — either way, not any task on this page.
systems.best_for: A starting point when the target ontology is closer to a 30-35-way word classification problem than a handful of binary/ternary decisions — its published numbers are on the larger label set most peer rows here don't attempt.
systems.watch: The published NGC checkpoint sits behind NVIDIA's NGC Terms of Use, a EULA distinct from the Apache-2.0 covering the training code itself — do not assume the checkpoint is Apache-licensed. Either way this is a backbone, not a classifier for this page's tasks, and the paper reports no device latency, only parameter counts and accuracy.
systems.standout: Its 1D time-channel-separable block design is inherited almost unchanged from QuartzNet, a full ASR architecture shrunk down — one of the few backbones here built by paring back a speech-recognition model rather than starting from an image-classification CNN.
systems.architecture: 1D time-channel-separable convolutions with residual connections, carried over from the QuartzNet ASR architecture rather than built from an image-classification CNN.
systems.accuracy_note: 97.21% (±0.067) on Google Speech Commands v1's 30-class task for the 77K-parameter MatchboxNet-3x1x64, per the paper (arXiv:2004.08531, Majumdar & Ginsburg, Interspeech 2020). 96.91% (±0.101) on v2's 35-class task for the same variant, rising to 97.37% (±0.110) at 140K parameters (MatchboxNet-6x2x64). Not the twelve-word task most peer rows use here — a larger label set, so not directly comparable to them either.
systems.verification_note: Read against the paper (arXiv:2004.08531) and NVIDIA's NeMo GitHub repository (Apache-2.0 LICENSE fetched and confirmed) and NGC catalog page for the published checkpoint, which states NGC Terms of Use govern it.

systems.name: Res8 / Res15 (Honk)
systems.task: No shipped classifier for any task on this page. A reference architecture for small acoustic classification, published against Google Speech Commands, that you instantiate and train on your own ontology.
systems.availability: Official implementation published (Castorini, University of Waterloo); the linked honk-models repository ships pretrained Caffe2/PyTorch checkpoints for the twelve-word Speech Commands keyword task, not any task on this page.
systems.best_for: The most heavily cited open baseline in this literature — TC-ResNet's own comparison table uses this exact res15 model (matching parameter count and accuracy almost to the decimal), and it remains the yardstick new small-footprint acoustic classifiers are measured against.
systems.watch: This is a backbone, not a classifier — code and any historical checkpoints are keyword-spotting only, on the same twelve-word task as most peer rows here. The paper reports parameter counts and multiply (MAC) counts, never a measured device latency; do not read the multiply count as a speed figure.
systems.standout: At publication, res15 was a drop-in replacement for Google's own Sainath & Parada CNN baseline on the identical task, beating it outright (95.8% vs. 91.7%) at roughly a fifth of the parameters — the paper explicitly frames itself as establishing "an open-source state-of-the-art reference" for others to build on, which is exactly how TC-ResNet and others have used it since.
systems.params: 19.9k (res8-narrow) to 438k (res26); the two variants most commonly cited elsewhere in this literature are res8 (110k) and res15 (238k)
systems.architecture: Deep residual CNN over stacked MFCC frames. The base res15 variant uses dilated convolutions to reach a large receptive field without added depth; the compact res8 variant trims to three residual blocks plus average-pooling instead.
systems.accuracy_note: 95.8% (±0.48) on Google Speech Commands (2017 release)'s 12-word task for the 238K-parameter res15, and 94.1% (±0.35) for the 110K-parameter res8, per the paper's own Table 4 (arXiv:1710.10361, five-run 95% CIs). The narrowest configuration, res8-narrow (19.9K parameters), reaches 90.1% (±0.98). A twelve-word task; says nothing about a conversational ontology.
systems.verification_note: Read against the paper (arXiv:1710.10361, Tang & Lin, ICASSP 2018) and the official MIT-licensed repository, castorini/honk (LICENSE fetched and confirmed). Cross-checked against TC-ResNet's own Table 1 baseline figures for this same res15 model (239K params, 95.8%, 424 ms on a Google Pixel 1) — the two papers' numbers for the identical model agree.

systems.name: TC-ResNet
systems.task: No shipped classifier for any task on this page. A reference architecture for small acoustic classification, published against Google Speech Commands, that you instantiate and train on your own ontology.
systems.availability: Official implementation published (Hyperconnect); the repository trains and evaluates keyword-spotting checkpoints on Speech Commands, not any task on this page.
systems.best_for: The fastest published option here when device latency is the binding constraint — designed and measured specifically for real-time inference on a phone CPU rather than optimised for parameter count alone.
systems.watch: This is a backbone, not a classifier — the repository trains and evaluates keyword-spotting checkpoints only. Parameter counts are a screening metric; the 1.1 ms figure is real but is 2019-era-phone-specific and says nothing about latency on today's hardware or a conversational ontology.
systems.standout: Reports measured on-device latency (Google Pixel 1) rather than only parameter/FLOP counts, which is unusual in this literature and is what makes its speedup claim checkable rather than asserted.
systems.architecture: 1D temporal convolution over stacked MFCC frames treated as a sequence, rather than a 2D image-style spectrogram convolution — the source of both its speed and its name.
systems.input_features: MFCC (40-dim, stacked as a 1D temporal sequence)
systems.latency_note: 1.1 ms per inference on a Google Pixel 1 for TC-ResNet8, per the paper — against 424 ms for the "Res15" CNN baseline (Tang & Lin's res15, the same model covered in this page's Res8/Res15 row) measured on the same device, the basis of the paper's "385x speedup" headline. Device- and paper-specific; not a general latency claim.
systems.accuracy_note: 96.1% on Google Speech Commands v1's 12-word task for the 66K-parameter TC-ResNet8, rising to 96.6% for the 305K-parameter TC-ResNet14-1.5, per the paper's own Table 1 (arXiv:1904.03814). A twelve-word task; says nothing about a conversational ontology.
systems.verification_note: Read against the paper (arXiv:1904.03814, Choi et al., Interspeech 2019) and the official Apache-2.0 repository, hyperconnect/TC-ResNet (LICENSE fetched and confirmed).

systems.name: Cyberon DSpotter / CSpotter
systems.licence: Proprietary — commercial licence from Cyberon Corporation, issued as chipset-tied licence files (free trial licence available)
systems.price_note: Not published — quote-based commercial licence from Cyberon or via silicon partners (Renesas, NXP, Infineon, XMOS); free trial license available, production licence files are issued per chipset ID
systems.task: Binary detection of a phoneme-authored custom wake word or voice command from continuous on-device audio.
systems.availability: Targets Arm Cortex-M MCUs and DSP/SoC platforms (CEVA, Tensilica, RISC-V via Andes); shipped through silicon-partner ecosystems including Renesas RA/RX, Infineon PSoC 6, NXP, GreenWaves, and XMOS xcore.
systems.best_for: MCU and silicon vendors, and OEMs building wake word plus on-device voice commands into cost- and power-constrained embedded hardware, where new commands need to be authored from text rather than recorded speech.
systems.watch: Pricing and licence terms are not published anywhere — every source (Cyberon's own site and every silicon-partner page) routes to 'contact sales' for a quote, so cost cannot be compared up front, and no independently measured accuracy figure was found to check the qualitative 'high accuracy' claim against.
systems.standout: Wake words and voice commands are authored purely by typing the phrase into a phoneme-based acoustic model — no recorded training corpus is needed for a new command — and its published footprint (as low as ~200KB flash / ~24KB RAM, scaling with vocabulary) targets true microcontrollers rather than app processors.
systems.model_size: DSpotter: roughly 200KB + 42B-per-command flash and 24KB + 130B-per-command RAM, scaling with vocabulary size, per Renesas' partner documentation of the product.
systems.architecture: Phoneme-based, speaker-independent neural keyword spotting for wake word plus local voice-command recognition; DSpotter targets MCU-class hardware, CSpotter adds on-device user-trained voice tags and speaker verification.
systems.custom_wake_word: Yes — DSpotter/CSpotter wake words and voice commands are defined by typing the phrase (phoneme-based acoustic model), with no voice-data collection required for new commands; CSpotter additionally supports on-device user-trained voice tags and speaker verification. Vendor states 26+ languages supported, expanding roughly 4 languages/month.
systems.verification_note: Footprint numbers are sourced from Renesas' partner documentation of Cyberon's product; qualitative accuracy and noise-robustness claims are Cyberon's own marketing language and were not independently benchmarked. No adoption/unit figures were found to cite.

systems.name: microWakeWord
systems.task: Binary detection of one or more fixed wake phrases, running entirely on the microcontroller from streaming audio.
